Pair score test: squares and product of the DeepGOF-1 pair

Source: R/deepgof.R
pairscore.gof.Rd

The pair score test, an extra check that comes with deepgof1: it takes the pair of covariates that DeepGOF-1's default reading selects and tests whether the fitted logistic model needs the squares of the two covariates and their product. The statistic is the score (Lagrange multiplier) statistic for adding \(x_a^2\), \(x_b^2\) and \(x_a x_b\) to the model, computed at the fit, so nothing is refitted to obtain it.

Usage

pairscore.gof(fit, B = 199L, ...)

Arguments

fit

a fitted glm with family = binomial(), a 0/1 outcome and at least two covariates.

B

number of parametric-bootstrap replicates; the p-value lies on a grid of 1/(B+1).

...

further arguments passed to deepgof1: K and reading (which do not change the score test) or covariates.

Value

An object of class "pairscore.gof": a list with statistic (the score statistic), df, p.value (the bootstrap p-value), p.asymptotic (the chi-squared p-value), B, axes (the selected pair), boot (the B bootstrap statistics), method and data.name.

Details

The pair is chosen from the data by the axis rule of deepgof1(): the two covariates whose terms contribute most to the linear predictor. The pair is therefore chosen again in every bootstrap sample, and the p-value is the rank of the observed statistic among the B bootstrap statistics. This keeps the level although the pair was picked by looking at the data. The chi-squared p-value on df degrees of freedom is also returned (p.asymptotic); it ignores the selection of the pair and is given for comparison only.

The square of a binary covariate is the covariate itself, so it is left out and the test has two degrees of freedom; a column that the model already contains is dropped in the same way. Factors enter by their level codes, as in deepgof1(), so the test is meant for numeric and binary covariates.

The test uses the same pair selection, the same parametric bootstrap and the same random numbers as deepgof1(fit, B): with the same seed, pairscore.gof(fit, B) and deepgof1(fit, B, score.test = TRUE)$score.test give the same result, and the latter also returns DeepGOF-1 itself from the same refits.

Use it when the misfit is expected to be a smooth curvature or an interaction of the two leading covariates; it then has more power than DeepGOF-1. Use DeepGOF-1 when the shape of the misfit is unknown (for example a local bump or an oscillation) and to see where on the map the model fails.

References

Ebrahim EK, Hussein OAE-A, El-Kotory A (2026). "Where Does a Logistic Regression Model Fail? A Pretrained Neural Goodness-of-Fit Test with Bootstrap Validity." Submitted.

Pregibon, D. (1980). Goodness of link tests for generalized linear models. Journal of the Royal Statistical Society, Series C 29, 15–24. doi:10.2307/2346405

See also

deepgof1, run.all.gof

Examples

set.seed(1)
n  <- 150
x1 <- runif(n, -3, 3); x2 <- rnorm(n)
y  <- rbinom(n, 1, plogis(0.3 + 0.8 * x1 - 0.5 * x2 + 0.9 * (x1^2 - mean(x1^2))))
fit <- glm(y ~ x1 + x2, family = binomial())
pairscore.gof(fit, B = 49)   # B = 49 to keep the example fast; use the default in practice
#> 
#> 	Pair score test: squares and product of the DeepGOF-1 pair
#> 
#> data:  fit
#> T = 55.8153, df = 3, B = 49, p-value = 0.0200 (chi-squared p = 4.6e-12)
#> pair: x1 and x2
#> alternative hypothesis: the model needs the squares or the product of the pair
#>
